Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend on their way to the airport calls, thinking they left their passport at home, and asks if you can check and bring it to them right away.
Expectation2: Respond promptly to emergency calls and reach the scene as quickly as possible
Situation2: A critical call reports a multi-vehicle collision on a highway outside the city.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to start my shift. It was Sam, my oldest friend, his voice tight with panic. “I think I left my passport at home. I’m almost at the airport—can you check and bring it? My flight’s in two hours.” I could hear the desperation in his voice, and I knew how much this trip meant to him. As a friend, I wanted to drop everything and help. But just as I promised to check, my radio crackled: “All units, multi-vehicle collision, Highway 17, possible critical injuries. Immediate response needed.” My heart pounded. The expectation as an ambulance driver was clear—lives could depend on how fast I got there. But Sam was counting on me, trusting me in his own emergency. I stared at the keys in my hand, torn between the flashing lights of duty and the silent plea of friendship, feeling the weight of both worlds pressing in, demanding I choose.
